title: Root cause analysis and remediation plan for scheduler ↔ autotile interaction regression
creator: Asha Mehta
description:
Summary:
On 2026-03-09 we observed a sustained p95/p99 latency uplift across a subset of hosted inference endpoints serving autoregressive attention-heavy workloads. Root cause analysis shows a behavioral interaction between a recent scheduler change (more aggressive probing of alternate execution paths) and the attention autotile heuristic that selects tiling / kernel variants by sequence-length micro-patterns.

What happened (concise timeline):
- 2026-03-09 02:18 UTC: Canary rollout of scheduler probing tweak (change introduced to broaden kernel candidates for short-lived bursts).
- 2026-03-09 04:05 UTC: First signs of a latency shift on canaries for attention-dense models (p95 increased ~2.3x).
- 2026-03-09 05:30 UTC: Rollout progressed; production p95 spiked on certain customers with mixed-sequence workloads.
- 2026-03-09 06:00–08:00 UTC: Autoscaling masked some capacity pressure but increased batch evictions and KV-cache churn; error rate stayed low.
- 2026-03-09 09:00 UTC: Emergency rollback of scheduler probing change on affected pools; p95 returned close to baseline within 20–30 minutes.

Root cause (short):
The scheduler probing change introduced transient kernel probing for candidate kernels without sufficient affinity constraints. For attention layers, the autotile heuristic expects stable sequence-length locality to pick a quantized kernel optimized for the dominant pattern. The probing logic intermittently chose a different kernel variant (mixed-quant path) when probes overlapped with bursts of short-then-long sequences. This produced higher memory footprint per-request, caused batch-level memory pressure, and triggered eviction/recreate cycles in the runtime’s batch allocator — amplifying tail latency.

Why this is unique/difficult:
- The regression manifests only under mixed-sequence distributions (short prefix + long continuation) that are common in chat workloads with function/tool calling.
- The autotile heuristic uses lightweight histograms that can be misleading during bursty traffic; probes temporarily poisoned the histogram state.
- The failure mode increases cost (more GPU memory churn) without producing obvious correctness errors, so it can quietly degrade cost/latency SLAs.

Immediate mitigations applied:
- Emergency rollback of the probing change from canary and then production pools (completed 2026-03-09 09:00 UTC).
- Hotfix: add a soft-affinity override that prevents kernel variant switches for attention layers if histogram stability < 60s. Deployed to affected pools as a scoped patch (patch-id: rbw-hotfix-781499).
- Increased alerting sensitivity for p95 and batch-eviction metrics on attention-dense model routes.

Telemetry and repro work completed:
- Reproduction harness created that simulates mixed-sequence bursts and reproduces median->p95 amplification in local synthetic clusters. Notebook and run script saved (see links).
- Added new telemetry counters: kernel_variant_switch_count, autotile_histogram_entropy, per-batch_eviction_count.

Longer-term remediation plan (roadmap):
1) Kernel affinity policy (owner: Diego Ramos, due: 2026-03-21): implement strict affinity guardrails for attention kernels that consider both recent histogram stability and probe success rate.
2) Probing backoff protocol (owner: Priya Shah, due: 2026-04-04): redesign probe cadence to incorporate weighted recent-history and per-route probe budgets.
3) Autotile histogram improvement (owner: Linh Tran, due: 2026-04-11): replace simple decay histogram with windowed quantile sketching to avoid transient poisoning.
4) Nightly regression benchmark (owner: SRE team, due: 2026-03-28): add mixed-sequence workload to nightly perf suite with p95/p99 regression guards and automatic PR blocking.
5) Observatory drill (owner: Observability PM, due: 2026-03-31): dashboard and rerun playbook that surfaces correlation between kernel switches, KV cache churn, and batch evictions.
6) Canary policy tightening (owner: Release Eng, due: 2026-04-01): require focused canary workload coverage for scheduler heuristics touching kernel selection.

Action items (atomic):
- [A1] Add kernel_variant_switch_count to metric exporter and create alert (owner: Diego, ETA: 2d).
- [A2] Merge rbw-hotfix-781499 to stable and schedule redeploy (owner: Diego, ETA: 1d).
- [A3] Implement and unit test affinity guardrail (PR TBD) (owner: Diego, ETA: 10d).
- [A4] Add mixed-sequence case to nightly perf suite; gate PRs that touch scheduler (owner: SRE, ETA: 7d).
- [A5] Postmortem writeup and customer comms draft (owner: Asha, ETA: 3d).

Acceptance criteria for 'done':
- No p95 regressions observed for mixed-sequence workloads on canaries for 72h after planned rollout.
- Nightly benchmark fails PRs that cause >10% p95 regression vs baseline for the mixed-sequence test.
- Dashboards show kernel switch rate reduced by 90% in steady-state for attention layers.

Open questions and trade-offs:
- How aggressive should affinity be before we sacrifice opportunity to find a faster kernel on heterogeneous hardware? (balance performance vs stability)
- Should probes be per-route or per-worker? Per-route is safer but might hide good opportunities.
- How to tune histogram window vs memory overhead for sketches?

Bottom line:
This incident exposed a fragile interaction between scheduler probing and the attention autotile heuristic. Immediate rollback and a short-term guardrail mitigated customer impact. The plan centers on stronger affinity policies, better telemetry, and an explicit mixed-sequence regression test to prevent recurrence.
